claims.text: Local surface chemical composition governs the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Ni is a relatively high-melting-point constituent and Al is a relatively low-melting-point constituent.
Surfaces with more Ni and less Al have stronger interatomic bonding.
Stronger bonding at a Ni-rich surface delays the onset of surface premelting.
Stronger bonding at a Ni-rich surface elevates the overall nanoparticle melting temperature.
The initial AlCoCrFeNi nanoparticles have a nominally homogeneous, randomly mixed bulk composition.
The controlled comparison changes surface Ni/Al enrichment while keeping particle size, shape, overall bulk composition, atmosphere, heating rate, and other environmental conditions constant.
Local surface bonding interactions influence surface cohesive energy.
Ni atoms stabilize the nanoparticle surface more than Al atoms.
Surface compositional segregation modulates the local cohesive energy at the nanoparticle interface.
In Al-matrix composites reinforced with AlCoCrFeNi, interfaces containing more than 25% Ni or less than 20% Al are more stable.
In the cited Al/AlCoCrFeNi composite interfaces, Ni stabilizes the interface whereas Al deteriorates its stability.
Al enrichment lowers bonding strength and triggers earlier nanoparticle surface premelting.
Ni-enriched nanoparticles will have higher premelting-onset and overall melting temperatures than Al-enriched nanoparticles.
The melting-temperature difference could be tens of degrees Celsius.
A few to tens of nanometers is a typical nanoparticle size range for catalysis and sensing.
The proposed relationship may fail for very small clusters or HEAs with substantially different constituent metals.
The magnitude of the surface-composition effect may vary with particle size, synthesis method, and alloy system.
XPS or atom-probe tomography can be used to verify the intended surface compositions, while in situ TEM and DSC can measure premelting and melting behavior.

Failure of the Ni-enriched particles to show statistically higher premelting-onset and melting temperatures than the Al-enriched particles, or observation of greater stability for Al-enriched particles, would falsify the hypothesis.
